description: Core classic menswear knowledge base. Contains color theory, fit and proportion rules, garment histories and pairings, proven outfit combinations, style family systems (Ivy, Prep, Americana, Military, Workwear), timeless principles, and a 110-rule master rulebook. Extracted from foundational menswear literature.
source_books: A Dictionary of Color Combinations — Sanzo Wada
Permanent Style Presents: The Style Guide
Icons of Men's Style — Josh Sims

harmony_principles.description: Build every outfit on at least one neutral: navy, black, white, gray, beige, tan, cream, or khaki.
harmony_principles.why_it_works: Neutrals absorb color without clashing and provide visual stability.
harmony_principles.when_to_use: Always — as base for trousers, jacket, or shirt.
harmony_principles.when_to_avoid: Avoid all-neutral when you want personality or visual interest.
examples: Navy trousers + white shirt
Gray trousers + beige jacket
Black jeans + white tee

harmony_principles.description: Limit a full outfit to three colors maximum.
harmony_principles.why_it_works: More than three colors fragments the eye and makes the outfit look accidental.
harmony_principles.when_to_use: All outfits, especially smart casual and formal.
harmony_principles.when_to_avoid: Festival or expressive streetwear contexts may break this.
examples: Navy + white + brown
Gray + burgundy + white
Olive + tan + cream

harmony_principles.description: 60% dominant color, 30% secondary color, 10% accent color.
harmony_principles.when_to_use: Smart casual, business casual, and formal outfits.
harmony_principles.when_to_avoid: Casual/streetwear where rules are more fluid.
examples: Navy (60%) trousers + white (30%) shirt + burgundy (10%) pocket square

harmony_principles.description: Colors adjacent on the color wheel work together: blue + teal + green, or red + orange + brown.
harmony_principles.why_it_works: Adjacent colors share undertones, creating a cohesive look.
examples: Olive shirt + tan chinos + brown boots
Navy jacket + teal shirt + gray trousers

harmony_principles.description: Colors opposite on the wheel create strong, intentional contrast: navy + mustard, burgundy + olive, purple + orange.
harmony_principles.why_it_works: Opposing hues make each other appear more vivid.
harmony_principles.when_to_use: When you want a bold, deliberate look.
examples: Navy jacket + mustard trousers
Burgundy shirt + olive trousers

harmony_principles.description: Wear different shades of the same color family head to toe.
harmony_principles.why_it_works: Creates a clean, elongated silhouette and appears deliberate.
harmony_principles.when_to_use: When you want a modern, minimal look.
harmony_principles.when_to_avoid: When tones clash within the same family (e.g., two different navies that don't match).
examples: Light gray shirt + mid gray trousers + charcoal shoes
Cream shirt + tan chinos + brown boots

neutral_combinations.note: The most reliable combination in menswear

colors_that_clash.reason: Both are dark base colors that compete
Both are dark base colors that muddy each other
Too close in hue, creates visual noise
Analogous but too similar in energy
Too similar in hue family without tonal separation

formal_color_rules: Stick to navy, charcoal, black, white, and gray for formal occasions
Avoid bright colors in formal business or black-tie settings
A white shirt is the most versatile formal shirt color
Light blue is the only acceptable color alternative to white in formal settings
Dark tie should contrast with light shirt; light tie with dark shirt
casual_color_rules: Casual contexts allow earth tones: olive, tan, rust, mustard, terracotta
Streetwear permits bold color blocking if limited to two tones
Denim acts as a neutral — it pairs with almost everything

shirt_fit_rules.description: The shirt shoulder seam must sit exactly at the shoulder bone edge — not hanging over the arm, not pulled inward.
shirt_fit_rules.why_it_works: The shoulder is the structural foundation of any upper garment. A misaligned shoulder makes everything else look wrong.
examples: If seam hangs 1 inch past shoulder = too large
If seam pulls toward neck = too small

shirt_fit_rules.description: When buttoned at the top, you should be able to fit two fingers comfortably between collar and neck.
shirt_fit_rules.why_it_works: Too tight restricts movement and looks uncomfortable; too loose looks sloppy.
examples: One finger too tight for comfort
Four fingers = collar too wide

shirt_fit_rules.description: Untucked: shirt hem should fall mid-crotch level. Tucked: long enough to stay tucked through full range of motion.
shirt_fit_rules.why_it_works: Too short untucked looks abbreviated; too long looks like a dress.
examples: Oxford shirt untucked should end around hip pocket level

shirt_fit_rules.description: Half inch of shirt cuff must show below jacket sleeve.
shirt_fit_rules.why_it_works: Shows intentionality and polish; a detail that signals careful dressing.
shirt_fit_rules.when_to_use: Formal and business contexts with a jacket.
examples: Navy jacket + white shirt with 0.5 inch cuff showing

jacket_fit_rules.description: Jacket shoulders must be perfectly aligned to shoulder bone. No divots, no shoulder pad overhang.
jacket_fit_rules.why_it_works: The shoulder is the most expensive alteration — if it doesn't fit here, no tailor can fully fix it.
examples: A ripple at the top of the sleeve cap = wrong shoulder width

jacket_fit_rules.description: When the jacket is buttoned, there should be no X-shaped pulling at the button.
jacket_fit_rules.why_it_works: X-shaped pull means the jacket is too tight across the chest.
examples: Always unbutton jacket when sitting to prevent pull

jacket_fit_rules.description: Jacket sleeve should end at the wrist bone, showing 0.5 inch of shirt cuff.
jacket_fit_rules.why_it_works: The cuff detail finishes the arm line and signals precision.
examples: Navy blazer with white shirt — small white cuff always visible

jacket_fit_rules.description: Jacket hem should cover the seat of your trousers and your knuckles when arms hang naturally.
jacket_fit_rules.why_it_works: Correct length maintains visual balance between upper and lower body.
examples: A too-short jacket makes legs look short; too long makes torso look long

trouser_fit_rules.description: Full break = fabric pools on shoe. Half break = slight fold at shoe. No break = hem above shoe top.
trouser_fit_rules.why_it_works: Break affects the formality and modernity of the silhouette.
trouser_fit_rules.when_to_use: No break or half break for modern/slim fits; full break for classic formal.
examples: Slim chinos with no break look modern
Wide-leg trousers with full break look classic

trouser_fit_rules.description: Trousers should sit at natural waist without a belt to hold them up.
trouser_fit_rules.why_it_works: A belt should be decorative, not structural. If needed to hold up trousers, they're too large.
examples: Chinos that sag without a belt = wrong size

trouser_fit_rules.description: Slim fit: fabric touches thigh lightly. Regular: light drape. Relaxed: visible drape.
trouser_fit_rules.why_it_works: Thigh fit determines overall silhouette and movement comfort.
examples: Skinny jeans hug thigh completely
Relaxed chinos drape naturally

visual_balance_rules.description: One fitted item + one relaxed item. Never oversized top + oversized bottom.
visual_balance_rules.why_it_works: Volume on both top and bottom loses all silhouette definition.
examples: Oversized hoodie + slim jeans
Wide-leg trousers + fitted turtleneck

visual_balance_rules.description: Avoid long jackets, long shorts, or wide breaks on trousers. Keep proportions tight.
visual_balance_rules.why_it_works: Long vertical lines are cut by wide horizontal breaks — shortening visual height.
examples: Cropped jackets, no-break trousers, and slim cuts elongate shorter frames

visual_balance_rules.description: Tall men can carry longer jackets, wider trousers, and more volume.
visual_balance_rules.why_it_works: Height gives room to absorb extra fabric without losing structure.
examples: Wide-leg trousers and longer overcoats look intentional on tall frames

oxford_shirt.purpose: Casual smart shirt — the most versatile shirt in menswear
oxford_shirt.history: Originated at Oxford University in the 1800s, adopted by Ivy League students in America
typical_mistakes: Buttoning all the way up without a tie

denim_jacket.purpose: Casual layering piece — functions as a light outerwear option
denim_jacket.history: Evolved from Levi's workwear in the 1880s, became a youth culture symbol in the 1950s-80s
typical_mistakes: Wearing oversized when outfit is already loose

chinos.purpose: The bridge between formal trousers and casual jeans
chinos.history: Military origin (British India, 1840s), adopted into American Ivy style in the 1950s
typical_mistakes: Pairing with very formal shirt and tie

jeans.purpose: Casual bottom — the most democratic garment in modern dressing
jeans.history: Levi Strauss workwear patent 1873, became fashion item in the 1950s through James Dean
jeans.formality_level: Casual to smart casual (dark wash only)
typical_mistakes: Light wash jeans in smart casual context
Pairing with blazer and light wash

polo_shirt.purpose: Sport-casual shirt that bridges athleisure and smart casual
polo_shirt.history: René Lacoste invented it for tennis in 1926, adopted into preppy American style in the 1950s

loafers.purpose: Slip-on shoe that bridges casual and smart casual effortlessly
loafers.history: Norwegian fishermen's shoe adopted by American prep culture in the 1930s-50s
typical_mistakes: Wearing with thick socks (penny loafers need no-show socks or bare ankle)

boots.purpose: Versatile footwear with heritage roots — adds ruggedness and edge
boots.history: Military and workwear origins; Chelsea boot popularized in 1960s London
boots.formality_level: Casual to smart casual (Chelsea boots reach business casual)
typical_mistakes: Pairing chunky work boots with tailored trousers

trench_coat.purpose: Classic outerwear that elevates any outfit beneath it
trench_coat.history: Burberry created it for WWI British officers in 1914; became a fashion icon post-war

bomber_jacket.purpose: Military-heritage casual outerwear with clean, versatile silhouette
bomber_jacket.history: US Air Force MA-1 flight jacket, adopted into streetwear and fashion in the 1980s-90s
typical_mistakes: Pairing with other loud statement pieces

blazer.purpose: The single most versatile tailored garment — dresses up or down
blazer.history: Originated in British boating culture (1820s), evolved into a wardrobe staple through Ivy League influence
blazer.formality_level: Smart casual to business casual to semi-formal
typical_mistakes: Matching it too perfectly (becomes a suit)
Pairing with casual trainers in formal context

knitwear.purpose: Layering piece that adds warmth, texture, and depth
knitwear.formality_level: Casual to smart casual (fine-gauge wool reaches business casual)

part4_outfit_combination_rules.why_it_works: Both garments have the same level of formality and casualness — they were made for each other.
part4_outfit_combination_rules.notes: Roll sleeves slightly for a relaxed feel. Tuck in for smarter occasions.

part4_outfit_combination_rules.combination: Denim jacket + white tee + dark jeans + boots
part4_outfit_combination_rules.why_it_works: Classic American heritage look. The contrast between the denim jacket and dark jeans works because the washes are different.
part4_outfit_combination_rules.notes: Never match the wash of jacket and jeans — always use different indigo tones.

part4_outfit_combination_rules.combination: Navy blazer + gray trousers + white shirt
part4_outfit_combination_rules.why_it_works: The navy/gray/white trio is the most reliable combination in menswear. Each color occupies a different tone level.
part4_outfit_combination_rules.notes: Add a pocket square for formal occasions. Remove tie for smart casual.

part4_outfit_combination_rules.why_it_works: A preppy formula that has never failed — all three items share the same casual-smart register.
part4_outfit_combination_rules.notes: Tuck polo into chinos for smarter look. Keep colors in the same tonal family.

part4_outfit_combination_rules.why_it_works: Turtleneck replaces shirt and tie simultaneously — elegant and modern.
part4_outfit_combination_rules.notes: Stick to fine-gauge wool or cashmere for smarter occasions. Chunky knit = more casual.

part4_outfit_combination_rules.combination: Bomber jacket + slim jeans + clean white sneakers
part4_outfit_combination_rules.why_it_works: All three items sit in the same casual-contemporary register. The silhouette is balanced: fitted jacket, slim bottom, minimal shoe.
part4_outfit_combination_rules.notes: Keep colors simple — the combination is enough. One muted tone and two neutrals.

part4_outfit_combination_rules.why_it_works: The trench coat's heritage and length complement the suit perfectly. Both items were designed for formal urban wear.
part4_outfit_combination_rules.notes: Belt the trench coat — leaving it unbuttoned looks unfinished.

ivy.core_philosophy: Relaxed American collegiate elegance — dressed up but never trying too hard.
typical_outfit_formulas: Oxford shirt + khaki chinos + penny loafers
Polo shirt + navy chinos + white sneakers
V-neck sweater + oxford shirt + gray flannel trousers + loafers

prep.core_philosophy: East Coast American upper-class aesthetics — polished, heritage, never flashy.
typical_outfit_formulas: Cable-knit sweater + collared shirt + chinos + loafers

americana_heritage.core_philosophy: Workwear and utility roots — honest, durable, functional clothing with character.
typical_outfit_formulas: Flannel shirt + raw denim jeans + work boots
Chambray shirt + khaki chinos + desert boots
Denim jacket + white tee + dark jeans + boots

military_inspired.core_philosophy: Structured, utilitarian dressing with purpose-built garments repurposed for civilian wear.
typical_outfit_formulas: Field jacket + white tee + cargo pants + boots

workwear.core_philosophy: Durable, functional clothing elevated through quality materials and fit.
typical_outfit_formulas: Chore coat + plain tee + jeans + work boots
Overshirt + white tee + cargo pants + boots

part6_timeless_principles.explanation: A well-fitted garment from a budget brand always looks better than a poorly fitted luxury piece. Fit is the first thing the eye registers.
Trend-driven clothing looks dated within 2-3 years. Simple, well-constructed basics remain relevant for decades.
Clothes are not seen in isolation. Every color interacts with the one next to it. Understanding this interaction is the foundation of dressing well.
The best outfit is the one appropriate for the occasion. Overdressing and underdressing are both mistakes.
A wardrobe of 20 high-quality, versatile items will serve you better than 100 mediocre pieces.

part6_timeless_principles.principle: The shoulder is the foundation of tailoring
part6_timeless_principles.explanation: Every other dimension of a jacket flows from the shoulder fit. It is also the hardest to alter. Always buy for the shoulder first.

part6_timeless_principles.principle: Neutrals are the backbone of a wardrobe
part6_timeless_principles.explanation: Navy, gray, white, beige, and black are interchangeable and combinable. Building around these maximizes outfit combinations.

part6_timeless_principles.principle: Texture adds interest without color risk
part6_timeless_principles.explanation: When unsure about color combinations, introduce texture: tweed, knit, corduroy, suede. Texture variation within the same color family is always safe.
If you wear something bold — a patterned shirt, a bright jacket, an unusual shoe — keep everything else simple. Let one piece speak.
Garments with long histories (oxford shirts, denim, trench coats, loafers) remain in style because they solved real problems and were refined over generations.
Dressing well is a skill developed through observation, study, and practice — not something you are born with.

part6_timeless_principles.principle: American style was built on appropriation and refinement
part6_timeless_principles.explanation: American menswear absorbed British, Italian, and workwear traditions and refined them into relaxed, democratic forms.

part7_master_rulebook: Rule 1: Fit matters more than brand or price.
Rule 2: The shoulder seam of any jacket or shirt must sit exactly at the shoulder bone.
Rule 3: Build every outfit around at least one neutral color.
Rule 4: Limit any outfit to a maximum of three colors.
Rule 5: Follow the 60-30-10 rule: 60% dominant, 30% secondary, 10% accent.
Rule 6: Never pair navy and black in the same outfit.
Rule 7: Never pair brown and black in the same outfit.
Rule 8: White is the most versatile shirt color in any wardrobe.
Rule 9: Navy is the most versatile trouser and jacket color in any wardrobe.
Rule 10: One bold pattern in an outfit is enough — everything else should be solid.
Rule 11: Stripes pair only with solids, never with other patterns.
Rule 12: Checks and plaids pair only with solids.
Rule 13: Denim acts as a neutral — it pairs with almost any color.
Rule 14: Never match denim jacket and denim jeans of the same wash.
Rule 15: Volume balance is essential — if the top is oversized, the bottom must be slim.
Rule 16: Never wear oversized top and oversized bottom simultaneously.
Rule 17: Dress for the occasion first, personal style second.
Rule 18: Overdressing is always preferable to underdressing in ambiguous situations.
Rule 19: A well-fitted inexpensive suit beats a poorly-fitted expensive one.
Rule 20: The collar point length should be proportional to tie width and lapel width.
Rule 21: Shirt cuff must show 0.5 inch below jacket sleeve in formal contexts.
Rule 22: Trouser break should be no break or half break for modern slim fits.
Rule 23: Trousers should sit at the natural waist without a belt to hold them up.
Rule 24: Shoes should be darker than or the same tone as trousers — never lighter.
Rule 25: Match belt color to shoe color in formal contexts.
Rule 26: Sneakers are not acceptable footwear at interviews, formal dinners, or weddings.
Rule 27: Flip flops are beach-only footwear.
Rule 28: Loafers are the most versatile smart-casual shoe.
Rule 29: Chelsea boots are the most versatile smart-casual boot.
Rule 30: Oxford shoes are the most formal shoe type.
Rule 31: Blazers can be dressed up with trousers and down with dark jeans.
Rule 32: A navy blazer is the single most versatile outer garment in menswear.
Rule 33: A blazer should never be mistaken for the jacket of a suit.
Rule 34: Polo shirts are not appropriate for formal business settings.
Rule 35: Oxford shirts are appropriate from casual to smart-casual only.
Rule 36: Dress shirts are appropriate from smart-casual to formal.
Rule 37: Graphic t-shirts are casual garments and should not be worn with tailoring.
Rule 38: Turtlenecks can replace a shirt and tie in semi-formal settings.
Rule 39: A white t-shirt under an open-collar dress shirt is always acceptable.
Rule 40: Roll shirt sleeves to the elbow to signal relaxed intent.
Rule 41: Knitwear adds texture without color complexity.
Rule 42: V-neck sweaters should always show a collar beneath them.
Rule 43: Cardigans layer over collared shirts for a smart-casual result.
Rule 44: Turtleneck + blazer is a timeless alternative to shirt + tie.
Rule 45: Trench coats elevate any outfit worn beneath them.
Rule 46: Bomber jackets belong in casual and smart-casual outfits only.
Rule 47: Parka is casual outerwear and should not be worn over formal attire.
Rule 48: Field jackets pair best with jeans, chinos, and casual trousers.
Rule 49: Overcoats are the most elegant form of outerwear.
Rule 50: Chinos are the bridge between jeans and formal trousers.
Rule 51: Cargo pants are casual garments — avoid with tailored or smart pieces.
Rule 52: Joggers and sweatpants belong in athleisure and gym contexts only.
Rule 53: Wide-leg trousers require a fitted top to balance silhouette.
Rule 54: Slim trousers pair with both fitted and slightly relaxed tops.
Rule 55: Shorts are casual and season-specific — avoid in autumn and winter.
Rule 56: Bermuda shorts are the most versatile short length for smart casual.
Rule 57: Linen is the ideal summer fabric — breathable and textured.
Rule 58: Wool is the most versatile cold-weather fabric.
Rule 59: Cashmere signals quality without effort.
Rule 60: Denim is an all-season fabric at the casual end of the spectrum.
Rule 61: Leather and suede belong in autumn and winter primarily.
Rule 62: Polyester and nylon are functional but signal lower quality in tailoring contexts.
Rule 63: Cotton is the most universal casual fabric.
Rule 64: Silk and satin are formal fabrics — avoid in casual settings.
Rule 65: Earth tones work year-round but peak in autumn.
Rule 66: Pastels are spring and summer colors.
Rule 67: Deep tones — burgundy, forest green, navy — are autumn and winter colors.
Rule 68: White and cream are summer and spring staples but can work year-round.
Rule 69: Black is appropriate year-round but is most natural in formal and winter contexts.
Rule 70: Mustard and olive are versatile earthy tones that pair with navy, brown, and gray.
Rule 71: Burgundy pairs with navy, gray, beige, and cream.
Rule 72: Teal pairs with navy, gray, white, and beige.
Rule 73: Red is an accent color — use sparingly.
Rule 74: Gold hardware and gold tones pair with warm colors; silver with cool.
Rule 75: Monochromatic outfits (same color family) look intentional and modern.
Rule 76: Tonal dressing requires different shades of the same hue — not the exact same tone.
Rule 77: One statement piece per outfit — let it breathe.
Rule 78: Clothes should fit your current body, not the body you plan to have.
Rule 79: Quality shoes and quality outerwear are the highest return investments in a wardrobe.
Rule 80: Occasion always dictates the formality ceiling of an outfit.
Rule 81: Smart casual is not an excuse to wear whatever you like — it has its own rules.
Rule 82: Business casual requires no denim, no graphic tees, no athletic wear.
Rule 83: Formal occasions require dark shoes, no exposed denim, and structured outerwear.
Rule 84: Beach and gym wear must not cross into any other occasion category.
Rule 85: Religious events require modest, clean, and occasion-appropriate clothing.
Rule 86: Heritage garments (oxford shirts, chinos, loafers) are always safe choices.
Rule 87: Simplicity always ages better than trend-driven complexity.
Rule 88: A well-maintained wardrobe of 20 pieces beats a cluttered wardrobe of 100.
Rule 89: Texture adds visual depth without introducing color risk.
Rule 90: Mixing textures within the same color family is always safe.
Rule 91: Pattern scale matters — a large check and a small stripe can coexist if separated by a solid.
Rule 92: The Ivy formula (oxford shirt + chinos + loafers) is the most reliable casual outfit in menswear.
Rule 93: The navy blazer formula (blazer + gray trousers + white shirt) is the most reliable smart-casual outfit.
Rule 94: The Americana formula (white tee + dark jeans + boots) is the most reliable casual outfit.
Rule 95: Dressing well is a learnable skill — it improves with observation and practice.
Rule 96: Study what works, not just what you like.
Rule 97: Personal style is built on mastered basics, not avant-garde experiments.
Rule 98: The best dressed men look effortless because they have internalized the rules.
Rule 99: Always consider the full silhouette, not individual garments.
Rule 100: The purpose of clothing is to serve the person wearing it — not the other way around.
Rule 101: Occasion, color, fit, and proportion — master these four and everything else follows.
Rule 102: When in doubt, wear navy, white, and well-fitted basics.
Rule 103: Your shoes are the first thing people notice and the last thing you should compromise on.
Rule 104: Clothes communicate context — wear what sends the right message for where you are going.
Rule 105: Ivy and prep style families share the same DNA: oxford cloth, chinos, loafers, and blazers.
Rule 106: Military-inspired garments (bombers, parkas, field jackets) belong in casual registers only.
Rule 107: Workwear and heritage garments earn credibility through age and patina — buy quality and wear it.
Rule 108: American style is democratic — it works for every body type when the fit is correct.
Rule 109: Never sacrifice comfort entirely for aesthetics — discomfort affects posture and confidence.
Rule 110: A great outfit starts with clean, well-maintained, properly stored garments.
